source_text:
CHAPTER XLVII.
Check.


Tito’s clever arrangements had been unpleasantly frustrated by trivial
incidents which could not enter into a clever man’s calculations. It
was very seldom that he walked with Romola in the evening, yet he had
happened to be walking with her precisely on this evening when her
presence was supremely inconvenient. Life was so complicated a game
that the devices of skill were liable to be defeated at every turn by
air-blown chances, incalculable as the descent of thistle-down.

It was not that he minded about the failure of Spini’s plot, but he
felt an awkward difficulty in so adjusting his warning to Savonarola on
the one hand, and to Spini on the other, as not to incur suspicion.
Suspicion roused in the popular party might be fatal to his reputation
and ostensible position in Florence: suspicion roused in Dolfo Spini
might be as disagreeable in its effects as the hatred of a fierce dog
not to be chained.

If Tito went forthwith to the monastery to warn Savonarola before the
monks went to rest, his warning would follow so closely on his delivery
of the forged letters that he could not escape unfavourable surmises.
He could not warn Spini at once without telling him the true reason,
since he could not immediately allege the discovery that Savonarola had
changed his purpose; and he knew Spini well enough to know that his
understanding would discern nothing but that Tito had “turned round”
and frustrated the plot. On the other hand, by deferring his warning to
Savonarola until the morning, he would be almost sure to lose the
opportunity of warning Spini that the Frate had changed his mind; and
the band of Compagnacci would come back in all the rage of
disappointment. This last, however, was the risk he chose, trusting to
his power of soothing Spini by assuring him that the failure was due
only to the Frate’s caution.

Tito was annoyed. If he had had to smile it would have been an unusual
effort to him. He was determined not to encounter Romola again, and he
did not go home that night.

She watched through the night, and never took off her clothes. She
heard the rain become heavier and heavier. She liked to hear the rain:
the stormy heavens seemed a safeguard against men’s devices, compelling
them to inaction. And Romola’s mind was again assailed, not only by the
utmost doubt of her husband, but by doubt as to her own conduct. What
lie might he not have told her? What project might he not have, of
which she was still ignorant? Every one who trusted Tito was in danger;
it was useless to try and persuade herself of the contrary. And was not
she selfishly listening to the promptings of her own pride, when she
shrank from warning men against him? “If her husband was a malefactor,
her place was in the prison by his side”—that might be; she was
contented to fulfil that claim. But was she, a wife, to allow a husband
to inflict the injuries that would make him a malefactor, when it might
be in her power to prevent them? Prayer seemed impossible to her. The
activity of her thought excluded a mental state of which the essence is
expectant passivity.

The excitement became stronger and stronger. Her imagination, in a
state of morbid activity, conjured up possible schemes by which, after
all, Tito would have eluded her threat; and towards daybreak the rain
became less violent, till at last it ceased, the breeze rose again and
dispersed the clouds, and the morning fell clear on all the objects
around her. It made her uneasiness all the less endurable. She wrapped
her mantle round her, and ran up to the loggia, as if there could be
anything in the wide landscape that might determine her action; as if
there could be anything but roofs hiding the line of street along which
Savonarola might be walking towards betrayal.

If she went to her godfather, might she not induce him, without any
specific revelation, to take measures for preventing Fra Girolamo from
passing the gates? But that might be too late. Romola thought, with new
distress, that she had failed to learn any guiding details from Tito,
and it was already long past seven. She must go to San Marco: there was
nothing else to be done.

She hurried down the stairs, she went out into the street without
looking at her sick people, and walked at a swift pace along the Via
de’ Bardi towards the Ponte Vecchio. She would go through the heart of
the city; it was the most direct road, and, besides, in the great
Piazza there was a chance of encountering her husband, who, by some
possibility to which she still clung, might satisfy her of the Frate’s
safety, and leave no need for her to go to San Marco. When she arrived
in front of the Palazzo Vecchio, she looked eagerly into the pillared
court; then her eyes swept the Piazza; but the well-known figure, once
painted in her heart by young love, and now branded there by eating
pain, was nowhere to be seen. She hurried straight on to the Piazza del
Duomo. It was already full of movement: there were worshippers passing
up and down the marble steps, there were men pausing for chat, and
there were market-people carrying their burdens. Between those moving
figures Romola caught a glimpse of her husband. On his way from San
Marco he had turned into Nello’s shop, and was now leaning against the
door-post. As Romola approached she could see that he was standing and
talking, with the easiest air in the world, holding his cap in his
hand, and shaking back his freshly-combed hair. The contrast of this
ease with the bitter anxieties he had created convulsed her with
indignation: the new vision of his hardness heightened her dread. She
recognised Cronaca and two other frequenters of San Marco standing near
her husband. It flashed through her mind—“I will compel him to speak
before those men.” And her light step brought her close upon him before
he had time to move, while Cronaca was saying, “Here comes Madonna
Romola.”

A slight shock passed through Tito’s frame as he felt himself face to
face with his wife. She was haggard with her anxious watching, but
there was a flash of something else than anxiety in her eyes as she
said—

“Is the Frate gone beyond the gates?”

“No,” said Tito, feeling completely helpless before this woman, and
needing all the self-command he possessed to preserve a countenance in
which there should seem to be nothing stronger than surprise.

“And you are certain that he is not going?” she insisted.

“I am certain that he is not going.”

“That is enough,” said Romola, and she turned up the steps, to take
refuge in the Duomo, till she could recover from her agitation.

Tito never had a feeling so near hatred as that with which his eyes
followed Romola retreating up the steps.

There were present not only genuine followers of the Frate, but Ser
Ceccone, the notary, who at that time, like Tito himself, was secretly
an agent of the Mediceans.

Ser Francesco di Ser Barone, more briefly known to infamy as Ser
Ceccone, was not learned, not handsome, not successful, and the reverse
of generous. He was a traitor without charm. It followed that he was
not fond of Tito Melema.

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER I. OUTSIDE

‘No room!--Full up!’

He banged the door in my face.

That was the final blow.

To have tramped about all day looking for work; to have begged even for a job which would give me money enough to buy a little food; and to have tramped and to have begged in vain,--that was bad. But, sick at heart, depressed in mind and in body, exhausted by hunger and fatigue, to have been compelled to pocket any little pride I might have left, and solicit, as the penniless, homeless tramp which indeed I was, a night’s lodging in the casual ward,--and to solicit it in vain!--that was worse. Much worse. About as bad as bad could be.

I stared, stupidly, at the door which had just been banged in my face. I could scarcely believe that the thing was possible. I had hardly expected to figure as a tramp; but, supposing it conceivable that I could become a tramp, that I should be refused admission to that abode of all ignominy, the tramp’s ward, was to have attained a depth of misery of which never even in nightmares I had dreamed.

As I stood wondering what I should do, a man slouched towards me out of the shadow of the wall.

‘Won’t ’e let yer in?’

‘He says it’s full.’

‘Says it’s full, does ’e? That’s the lay at Fulham,--they always says it’s full. They wants to keep the number down.’

I looked at the man askance. His head hung forward; his hands were in his trouser pockets; his clothes were rags; his tone was husky.

‘Do you mean that they say it’s full when it isn’t,--that they won’t let me in although there’s room?’

‘That’s it,--bloke’s a-kiddin’ yer.’

‘But, if there’s room, aren’t they bound to let me in?’

‘Course they are,--and, blimey, if I was you I’d make ’em. Blimey I would!’

He broke into a volley of execrations.

‘But what am I to do?’

‘Why, give ’em another rouser--let ’em know as you won’t be kidded!’

The door slammed with the dull, decisive thud of bureaucratic finality.

I stood in the freezing drizzle of the Hammersmith night, calculating the precise rate at which a man’s core temperature drops when he has been walking for fourteen hours on a deficit of three thousand calories. To have scoured the grime-choked streets of London all day for labor was an expected hardship; to have stooped to petition a casual ward for a night on a plank bed was a tactical compromise. To be denied even that miserable sanctuary was merely a lesson in the unreliability of institutional safety nets.

As I mentally mapped the grim reality of my situation, a figure detached itself from the shadows of the brick wall.

“Won’t let you in, eh?”

I turned to assess the man. His shoulders were hunched against the damp, his hands buried deep in the pockets of ruined trousers. He was a veteran of the gutters, worn down to the sinew, reeking of wet wool and cheap gin.

“He claims it’s at capacity,” I replied, my voice steady despite the shivering that had begun to seize my chest.

The man offered a jagged, cynical grin. “That’s the standard deterrent at Fulham. They always say it’s full. Keeps the ledger clean and the workload light.”

I studied him. “You’re suggesting it’s a calculated falsehood? An administrative bluff to filter the weak?”

“I’m saying the bloke’s having a laugh at your expense. If there’s square footage, they’re legally bound to take you. If I were you, I’d ring the bell again and make him do his job.”

There was a certain dark logic to testing the defenses twice. I approached the heavy door and yanked the iron bell-pull. The door swung open almost immediately, revealing the same grizzled pauper who acted as gatekeeper. If he had been the Prime Minister himself, he could not have worn a heavier mantle of unearned authority.

“Here again?” he sneered. “What’s the tactical objective here? Think I’ve got nothing better to do than wait on the likes of you?”

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER II. INSIDE

I realised, and, so to speak, mentally photographed all the little details of the house in front of which I was standing with what almost amounted to a gleam of preternatural perception. An instant before, the world swam before my eyes. I saw nothing. Now I saw everything, with a clearness which, as it were, was shocking.

Above all, I saw the open window. I stared at it, conscious, as I did so, of a curious catching of the breath. It was so near to me; so very near. I had but to stretch out my hand to thrust it through the aperture. Once inside, my hand would at least be dry. How it rained out there! My scanty clothing was soaked; I was wet to the skin! I was shivering. And, each second, it seemed to rain still faster. My teeth were chattering. The damp was liquefying the very marrow in my bones.

And, inside that open window, it was, it must be, so warm, so dry!

There was not a soul in sight. Not a human being anywhere near. I listened; there was not a sound. I alone was at the mercy of the sodden night. Of all God’s creatures the only one unsheltered from the fountains of Heaven which He had opened. There was not one to see what I might do; not one to care. I need fear no spy.

The cold was a physical enemy, steadily liquefying the marrow in my bones and draining the last of my cellular energy. But the open window presented a tactical anomaly, and more importantly, a lifeline.

It was a ground-floor sash, thrown wide to the deluge. I had only to breach the perimeter to secure dry cover. There was no watch, no patrol, no sign of life in the immediate vicinity. Out here, I was at the mercy of the elements, another anonymous casualty waiting to be swept into the Thames. The tramp at the casual ward had surrendered his freedom to the constabulary in exchange for a warm cell. I preferred to maintain my operational independence.

Perhaps the villa was empty. Civilian carelessness was a luxury of the secure and the comfortable. I considered knocking to alert the occupants of their vulnerability, perhaps angling for a meager reward. But experience in a harder school had taught me the futility of relying on the gratitude of the comfortable classes. More likely, I would be turned over to the authorities as a vagrant. Better to appropriate the shelter and vanish before dawn.

I leaned over the low brick wall, testing the air. The thermal differential was immediate; warmth bled from the dark aperture. Moving with deliberate silence, I vaulted the barrier. The ground beneath my boots felt cemented and stable. I pressed myself against the exterior masonry, listening at the crevice. Complete silence. It defied logic that any homeowner would leave a ground-floor blind fully raised and the sash open in this weather, but the battlefield is largely dictated by the blunders of the enemy.

Tito's meticulous scheming had been rendered obsolete by a trifling accident, a variable too insignificant to factor into the calculus of a mastermind. Yet, fate conspired to place him walking beside Romola on this very evening, rendering her presence an insurmountable obstacle. Life remained a labyrinthine game where the sharpest strategies were routinely dismantled by the chaotic drift of circumstance, unpredictable as falling dandelion seeds. Tito cared little for the collapse of Spini's plot; rather, he faced a tactical dilemma: how to deliver warnings to both Savonarola and Spini without triggering suspicion. Alerting the friar immediately, following the delivery of the forged letters, would invite unfavorable conjecture regarding his motives. Conversely, approaching Spini instantly required confessing the truth—that Savonarola had altered his course—which Spini's sharp intellect would interpret solely as Tito's sudden reversal and sabotage of the operation. Delaying the warning to the friar until morning carried the high probability of losing the chance to stop Spini entirely, leaving the Compagnacci faction to return in a fury of thwarted ambition.

This was the risk Tito elected to accept, banking on his ability to soothe Spini by attributing the failure to the Friar's mere caution. Annoyed, though finding it difficult to suppress such emotion given his usual composure, Tito resolved to avoid further contact with Romola and declined to return home that night.

Inside the house, Romola sat vigil through the darkness, refusing to remove her garments. She listened as the rain intensified, a rhythmic drumming that she found strangely comforting; the tempestuous sky seemed a divine shield against human machinations, forcing men into paralysis. Yet, her own mind was besieged by a dual torment: profound uncertainty regarding her husband's actions and a gnawing doubt concerning her own complicity. What falsehoods might he have woven? What designs remained hidden from her view? Trusting Tito was perilous; to convince herself otherwise was futile. Was she not acting out of selfish pride by shrinking from the duty to warn others against him? *"If her husband was a criminal,"* she reasoned, *"her proper station was within the prison walls beside him."* That sentiment held weight, yet it did not absolve her. Could a wife permit her spouse to commit acts that would brand him a malefactor when she possessed the agency to intervene? Prayer felt impossible; her agitated thoughts precluded the necessary state of expectant passivity. As the night wore on, her imagination spun frantic scenarios of how Tito might evade her threats. Just as dawn approached, the violence of the storm subsided, the wind dispersing the clouds to reveal a clear morning that only exacerbated her unease.

Wrapping her mantle tighter, Romola rushed to the loggia, scanning the vast landscape as if some external detail might dictate her next move, though she suspected only rooftops hid the path toward the Palazzo Vecchio where Savonarola might walk toward treachery. Should she seek her godfather? Might he act preemptively to block Fra Girolamo from crossing the gates without explicit proof? But that might be too late. With fresh distress, Romola realized she had gleaned no concrete intelligence from Tito, and the hour had long passed seven. There was no alternative.

She descended the stairs, ignoring the sick members of her household, and stepped out onto the Via de' Bardi, heading swiftly toward the Ponte Vecchio. She intended to traverse the city's heart via the most direct route; furthermore, the great Piazza offered a slim chance of intercepting her husband. By some lingering hope, he might appear there, clarify the Friar's status, and render a trip to San Marco unnecessary. Upon reaching the courtyard of the Palazzo Vecchio, she peered eagerly into the colonnade, then swept her gaze across the Piazza. The familiar silhouette, once etched by youthful affection and now scarred by suffering, was absent. Undeterred, she pressed onward to the Piazza del Duomo.

The square teemed with activity: worshippers ascending and descending the marble steps, men pausing for conversation, vendors laden with goods. Amidst this throng, Romola spotted her husband. Having exited San Marco, he had diverted into Nello's shop and was now leaning casually against the doorpost. As she drew nearer, she observed him conversing with effortless nonchalance, holding his cap in one hand and tossing back his freshly combed hair. The jarring contrast between this display of ease and the bitter anxieties he had instilled convulsed her with indignation; the renewed vision of his hardness intensified her dread. Standing nearby were Cronaca and two other regulars of San Marco. A sudden resolve struck her: *"I will force him to speak before these witnesses."*

Her light step closed the distance before Tito could retreat, coinciding with Cronaca's announcement, "Here comes Madonna Romola." A subtle shock rippled through Tito's frame as he confronted his wife. She appeared gaunt from sleepless vigilance, yet a flash of intensity beyond mere worry ignited in her eyes.

"Has the Frate crossed the gates?" she demanded.

"No," Tito replied, feeling utterly powerless before her scrutiny. He summoned every ounce of self-command to maintain a facade of simple surprise.

"And are you certain he is not departing?" she pressed.

"I am certain he is not going."

"That suffices," Romola declared, turning up the steps to seek refuge within the Duomo, needing solitude to quell her agitation.

Tito harbored no emotion closer to hatred than the one tracking her ascent. Present among the crowd were not only devoted followers of the Friar but also Ser Ceccone, the notary. At that moment, like Tito, Ceccone operated covertly as an agent of the Medici. Ser Francesco di Ser Barone, universally despised as Ser Ceccone, lacked learning, good looks, success, and generosity. He was a traitor devoid of charisma, and consequently, he held no affection for Tito Melema.
